text: s appears to be ef- fective;19 the use of maximal doses, perhaps in combina- tion with an H2-antagonist at night, is advocated by some20 but evidence to support twice daily (double) dosing is lacking.19 As the altered epithelium is relatively less sensi- tive to acid, symptom control does not necessarily equate to suppression of reflux.20 There is a lack of good evidence that control of acid reflux produces anything other than limited regression of the abnormal epithelium, or alters the risk of progression to malignancy,19,20 although there are some results that suggest benefit.21,22 Some evidence sug- gests that additional chemoprevention with aspirin or an- other NSAID might offer benefits in reducing cancer risk,19,23 but this remains investigational. The roles of screening, surveillance, and endoscopic ablation therapy or photodynamic therapy (5-aminolaevulinic acid or por- fimer) remain matters of debate.17,19,20 In infants, gastro-oesophageal reflux is common but usu- ally resolves spontaneously with increasing age and re- quires no treatment. Occasionally, it may be associated with complications such as failure to thrive, oesophagitis, and pulmonary symptoms of acid regurgitation, but can be managed by upright positioning and the use of thickened foods; drug therapy is controversial,24 and the evidence base is poor.25 It has been suggested that where drug ther- apy is needed, an alginate-antacid combination may be ap- propriate initially;24 PPIs are probably safe but are not well studied in infants.25 Cisapride has been given24,25 but the risk of cardiotoxicity makes the use of cisapride in infants extremely problematic (see p.1720). Metoclopramide may have some benefit but again this must be weighed against the risk of adverse effects.26 Evidence of benefit with dom- peridone is poor,27 and it too has the potential for serious adverse effects, but restrictions on cisapride have led to its over-use.25 Erythromycin has been investigated in infants with food intolerance, though not in gastro-oesophageal reflux itself; there is a risk of promoting bacterial resist- ance from such use.25 Gastrointestinal Drugs 1697 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) Gastro-oesophageal reflux is commonly encountered dur- ing normal pregnancy, and is generally managed by life- style and dietary modifications.28 If drug therapy is re- quired, nonsystemically absorbed antacids or sucralfate should be tried first. If these are ineffective, ranitidine may be tried. Proton pump inhibitors are reserved for women with severe or complicated reflux disease,28 due to con- cerns about their safety in pregnancy
